The error in each of the iterations varies, which is partly explained by the randomness when a new matrix C is created for each equation, but it also relates to how each dataset is affected by the range for M in equation 4. In the last column in Table 1, the lower bounds of M for each location are all under the 0.2⋅N value that is used for the experiment, though some sets are closer to the limit than others. N is the same constant for each location (8640), thus it is shown that the bound is directly proportional to K. Location 2 has the highest lower bound of the datasets used here at 0.1855⋅N which is directly because it is the least sparse vector, as seen in the second column. To account for some of the variation in error, a value of M = 0.2⋅N would be ideal for compressed sensing with sampling vectors similar to those tested here. This provides an ample margin for sparsity variation and randomness while also keeping measurement size considerably small. In order to further compare the error for other scenarios, we incrementally change the value of M and analyze the behavior of the percent error for each location. In theory, the lowest value M that would produce a reasonable percent error (< 0.05) for all 6 locations would be 0.1855⋅N. As seen in Figure 7, the percent errors for each line exponentially decays for all locations and specifically approach 0 after 0.1855⋅N (marked with the vertical dotted line). All errors before this line are far greater than 0.05 with some reaching as high as a 0.3 error which will result in an unrepresentative reconstruction. CONCLUSION Typical uses of compressed sensing include image and audio signal compression13, but further explored utilization have been achieved in recent years to include all corners of science. 8 Applications stretching to seismic waves14 and financial trends15 have also been used, showing that compressed sensing can be used on many data types, as long as it is a one-dimensional signal. This exploration led to the concept of applying these techniques to emission collectors, and applicably current air sample methods with one-dimensional signals where little research has been presented.
